notes.meaning: After forty years of peace, the Israelites turned back to evil and worshipped false idols. Because of their rebellion, God allowed the Midianites to defeat and rule over them for seven years. This hardship was God's discipline to wake up His people and lead them back to Him.

The Midianites were so cruel that the Israelites fled from their homes into the mountains. They had to carve out shelters in dark caves, ravines, and rocky strongholds to survive. Turning away from God had stripped them of their peace, their homes, and their security.

Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, enemy raiders swarmed into the land. The Midianites joined with the Amalekites and other desert tribes from the east to attack. They waited until the grain was almost ready so they could steal the harvest.

The invaders spread out across the countryside all the way to Gaza near the sea coast, ruining every farm. They stole all the food and carried off every sheep, ox, and donkey they could find. Israel was left starving, with no livestock and no way to feed their families.

The raiders came with their tents and livestock in swarms that looked like a plague of locusts. They also brought vast herds of camels, which allowed them to strike quickly and travel far across the desert. They moved across the countryside like a wave, devouring everything in sight.

These yearly raids stripped Israel of its food and wealth until the nation was crushed by poverty. Broken and hungry, the people finally cried out to the Lord for rescue. Deep distress often reminds people to turn to God when nothing else will.

When the suffering Israelites called out to the Lord, He listened to their cry for help. Even though they had caused their own trouble through sin, God still cared about their pain. Before He sent a hero to rescue them, He addressed what had gone wrong in their hearts.

God responded by sending an unnamed prophet to speak His message to the people. The prophet reminded them how the Lord had rescued their ancestors from slavery in Egypt. True rescue begins when people hear God's truth and recognize why they need Him.

The Lord reminded Israel that He had delivered them from Pharaoh's army and from every other oppressor along the way. He had driven out the native tribes and given Israel this fertile land to live in. Everything they enjoyed had come as a gift from His hand.

God had commanded His people to honor Him alone and not to worship the false gods of the Amorites around them. In spite of all His kindness, they had disobeyed His clear words. Their current misery was the direct result of breaking their promise to follow the Lord.

The angel of the Lord came to the village of Ophrah and sat beneath a large oak tree. Nearby, Gideon was beating out wheat inside a sunken winepress to keep the food hidden from Midianite raiders. Working inside a pit was clumsy and slow, but it kept the grain safe from thieves.

The angel appeared to Gideon and greeted him, saying, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor." Gideon was hiding in fear, but the Lord spoke to what Gideon would become with divine help. God's presence is what transforms ordinary, fearful people into heroes of faith.

Gideon asked why such terrible troubles had struck Israel if the Lord was truly with them. He remembered stories of the great miracles in Egypt and felt that God had now abandoned them to Midian. He did not yet see that Israel's own unfaithfulness had brought on this disaster.

The Lord looked at Gideon with favor and commanded him to go and save Israel using the strength he had. God asked, "Am I not sending you?" showing that Gideon's mission rested on divine authority. When God calls someone to a task, His backing is all the power they need.

Gideon protested that his family group was the weakest in the tribe of Manasseh and that he was the least important person in his household. He could not imagine how someone so poor and insignificant could lead a national rescue. God often chooses the small and humble so that the victory clearly belongs to Him.

The Lord answered Gideon's doubts with a firm promise: "Surely I will be with you." He assured Gideon that he would defeat the entire Midianite army as easily as striking down a single man. Success in God's work does not come from large numbers, but from the Lord's presence.

Gideon asked for a miraculous sign to prove that his visitor was truly speaking on behalf of God. He did not ask out of stubborn unbelief, but because the task was huge and dangerous. He wanted to be certain of his caller before risking everything.

Gideon asked the visitor to wait under the tree while he went to fetch an offering of food. The Lord graciously agreed to stay until Gideon returned. God showed remarkable patience by waiting on a hesitant servant.

Gideon went inside and cooked a young goat and baked unleavened bread using a large measure of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, then brought the meal out to present it under the tree. This generous feast was an expression of high honor and hospitality.

The angel told Gideon to set the meat and bread on a nearby rock and to pour out the broth over them. Gideon followed the instructions without question. The meal was transformed from ordinary food into a sacred offering laid upon an altar.

The angel reached out the tip of his staff and touched the food, causing fire to flare up from the rock and consume it all. Right after the offering burned, the angel vanished completely from sight. This miraculous fire was a clear sign that God had accepted the offering and confirmed His call.

When the visitor vanished, Gideon realized he had met the angel of the Lord face to face. He cried out in terror because the Israelites believed that seeing God's holy presence would bring instant death. His awe turned into deep fear for his life.

The Lord spoke words of comfort to Gideon: "Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die." God calmed his terror and assured him that he was safe. Encountering God's holiness brings fear, but His grace brings peace.

Gideon built an altar there to honor the Lord and gave it the name "The LORD Is Peace." The stone altar stood as a lasting reminder that God had shown him mercy and spared his life. Resting in God's peace gave Gideon the courage he needed to obey.

That same night, the Lord commanded Gideon to take his father's bulls and pull down his father's altar to the false god Baal. He was also told to chop down the wooden Asherah pole, an idol carved to honor a Canaanite goddess. Before Gideon could lead the nation in battle, he had to clear out idolatry from his own home.

God instructed Gideon to build a proper altar to the Lord on top of the town stronghold. He was to sacrifice the second bull as a burnt offering, using the chopped-up Asherah pole for the fire. True worship of God had to replace the false worship that had corrupted the community.

Gideon took ten of his servants and carried out the Lord's orders during the night. He acted under cover of darkness because he was afraid of what his family and the townspeople would do to him. Even though his courage was mixed with fear, he still carried out God's command.

When the townspeople woke up the next morning, they discovered that Baal's altar was destroyed and the Asherah pole cut down. They also saw the new altar to the Lord with a sacrificed bull smoking on top. The town's idolatrous shrine had been overturned in a single night.

The people looked around in shock and asked each other who had wrecked their sacred place. After asking around, they discovered that Gideon was the one who had torn it down. Gideon's secret night mission was now out in the open.

The angry mob marched to Joash and demanded that he bring out his son to be executed. They were willing to kill a neighbor's son to defend an idol of wood and stone. Turning away from God had blinded them into defending false gods instead of justice.

Joash stood up to the crowd and asked why they were trying to fight on behalf of Baal. He argued that if Baal were really a living god, he should be able to defend himself against someone who smashed his altar. This sharp logic silenced the mob and saved Gideon's life.

Because of that event, Gideon was given the nickname Jerubbaal, which means "Let Baal contend with him." The name taunted the false god and reminded everyone that Baal had no power to strike back. What began as a challenge became a badge of honor for Gideon's stand against idols.

The armies of Midian, Amalek, and the eastern desert nomads gathered together and crossed the Jordan River. They set up camp in the broad Valley of Jezreel to begin their annual raids on Israel's crops. This massive invasion brought the long-awaited crisis to a head.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, clothing him with divine power, courage, and authority. He blew a ram's horn to sound the battle call, and his own clan of Abiezer rallied behind him. God's Spirit turned a fearful farmer into a bold leader of men.

Gideon sent runners across his own tribe of Manasseh and into the northern tribes of Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali. Men from all four tribes answered the call and marched out to join him. God moved across the northern region to unite His people for battle.

Gideon prayed to God as the troops assembled for war. He repeated God's promise that Israel would be saved through his hand, yet he asked for confirmation before marching into battle. Even with thousands of soldiers behind him, he knew victory depended entirely on God.

Gideon proposed a test by placing a bundle of sheep's wool on the open threshing floor overnight. He asked that dew fall only on the fleece while the surrounding ground remained bone dry. If this happened, he would know for certain that God was going to save Israel through him.

God granted the sign exactly as Gideon had asked. Early the next morning, Gideon got up and wrung out the fleece, collecting a whole bowl full of water while the surrounding ground was dry. The miracle gave him unmistakable evidence of God's presence.

Gideon spoke to God again and asked Him not to be angry for requesting one more test. Knowing that wool naturally attracts moisture, he asked for the reverse miracle: let the fleece stay dry while dew covered all the surrounding ground. He approached God with deep humility, aware that he was testing divine patience.

That night, God patiently performed the second miracle, leaving only the fleece dry while dew soaked the ground around it. This supernatural sign removed any remaining doubt about God's call and promise. God showed extraordinary kindness in meeting His servant's weak faith to prepare him for victory.
